interpretation: Aluminium toxicity likely and severe P fixation; liming essential for most crops
explanation: Soluble aluminium (and often manganese) reaches levels that damage roots, so crops take up little water and nutrients; phosphorus is strongly fixed by iron and aluminium; calcium and magnesium are usually deficient; legume nitrogen fixation and soil biological activity are reduced.
source: USDA Soil Survey Manual (Soil Science Division Staff 2017)

interpretation: Aluminium toxicity likely and P poorly available; liming strongly advised
explanation: Aluminium toxicity commonly restricts root growth of maize and beans; much of the phosphorus (including fertilizer P) is fixed and unavailable; calcium and magnesium are often low, so fertilizer responses are poor.
source: USDA Soil Survey Manual (Soil Science Division Staff 2017)

interpretation: Aluminium toxicity possible for sensitive crops; liming advised for maize and beans
explanation: Exchangeable aluminium may be present and can limit root growth of sensitive crops such as maize and beans; phosphorus availability is reduced; raising pH improves fertilizer use efficiency.
source: USDA Soil Survey Manual (Soil Science Division Staff 2017)

interpretation: Suitable for most crops; monitor and lime only for sensitive crops
explanation: Aluminium toxicity is rare and most nutrients are adequately available; only acid-sensitive crops (e.g. some legumes) are likely to benefit from liming.
source: USDA Soil Survey Manual (Soil Science Division Staff 2017)

interpretation: Near-optimal nutrient availability for most crops
explanation: Close to the ideal range for most crops including maize; nutrients are at or near their highest availability.
source: USDA Soil Survey Manual (Soil Science Division Staff 2017)

explanation: Nutrient availability and soil biological activity are generally good for most crops.
source: USDA Soil Survey Manual (Soil Science Division Staff 2017)

interpretation: P Zn and Fe availability starts to decline
explanation: As pH rises above neutral, phosphorus, zinc, iron and manganese become less available to crops.
source: USDA Soil Survey Manual (Soil Science Division Staff 2017)

interpretation: Micronutrient deficiencies likely; check salinity and sodicity
explanation: Zinc, iron, manganese and phosphorus deficiencies are common; high pH can indicate carbonates, salts or sodium that also affect soil structure.
source: USDA Soil Survey Manual (Soil Science Division Staff 2017)

interpretation: Very poor structure and water and nutrient retention; organic inputs a priority
explanation: Very little organic matter to hold water and nutrients, bind soil particles or feed soil organisms; soils crust and erode easily and respond poorly to fertilizer.
source: Hazelton & Murphy (2016) Interpreting Soil Test Results

interpretation: Poor fertility buffering; manure compost and residue retention advised
explanation: Low organic matter gives weak soil structure and limited water and nutrient holding; fertilizer is used inefficiently.
source: Hazelton & Murphy (2016) Interpreting Soil Test Results

interpretation: Below desirable levels; integrated organic plus mineral fertilizer advised
explanation: Limited water and nutrient holding; building organic matter improves fertilizer response, yields and drought resilience.
source: Hazelton & Murphy (2016) Interpreting Soil Test Results

interpretation: Adequate; maintain with residue retention and organic inputs
explanation: Enough organic matter to support soil structure, water retention and nutrient supply; continued organic inputs are needed to prevent decline under continuous cropping.
source: Hazelton & Murphy (2016) Interpreting Soil Test Results

explanation: Good structure, water holding and nutrient supply from organic matter, supporting active soil biology.
source: Hazelton & Murphy (2016) Interpreting Soil Test Results

interpretation: Typical of forest or high-altitude soils; protect from conversion and erosion
explanation: A large carbon store typical of forest or high-altitude soils; converting to cropland causes rapid carbon loss.
source: Hazelton & Murphy (2016) Interpreting Soil Test Results
